intro: You are going to read about a young teacher from Tashkent who crossed Russia by train.

passage: Last summer, Malika Yusupova, a 24-year-old teacher from Tashkent, made the longest train journey of her life. She travelled on the Trans-Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok. The trip is more than 9,000 kilometres long and takes almost a week. “My friends thought I was crazy,” she laughs. “They asked me, ‘Why don't you just fly?’”

Malika shared a small room on the train with three other passengers. At night, the seats became beds. Her only luggage was one backpack, because there was not much space. At the end of every carriage there was a big machine with hot water, so people made tea and noodles all day. The carriage was often crowded and noisy, but it was warm and quite comfortable.

The best thing, she says, was the people. “On the first day, everyone was a stranger. By the third day, we were like a family.” An old man from Omsk taught her card games, and a young mother shared her homemade bread and fish. Malika didn't speak Russian very well, so she used her hands and a lot of smiles.

Every few hours, the train stopped for twenty or thirty minutes. Passengers jumped off and bought hot food from women on the platform. Malika always checked the timetable on the wall first. “If you are late, the train leaves without you!” The train also crossed seven time zones, so she often didn't know the real time. On the fifth day, she saw Lake Baikal, the deepest lake in the world. “The view from the window was amazing. I took two hundred photos.”

When the train finally arrived at its destination, Malika felt sad. She bought a small wooden souvenir at the station and said goodbye to her new friends. “Flying is faster,” she says, “but on a train you really see a country. Next year I'm going to take the train across China.”
